definitionEn: the subjects that are studied in a school, college or course.
existingExample: Many argue that the school curriculum should include practical life skills such as managing money.

definitionEn: learning by repeating information until you remember it, rather than understanding it.
existingExample: Exam-driven systems are often criticised for encouraging rote learning at the expense of critical thinking.

definitionEn: the money paid for being taught, especially at a college or university.
existingExample: Some governments have abolished tuition fees in order to widen access to higher education.

definitionEn: connected with the skills and knowledge needed for a particular job.
existingExample: Vocational courses can equip young people with the skills that employers actually need.

definitionEn: the process of continuing to learn new skills and knowledge throughout adult life.
existingExample: Rapid technological change has made lifelong learning essential for most workers.

definitionEn: that must be done because of a rule or law.
existingExample: Physical education should remain a compulsory subject in secondary schools.

definitionEn: the ability to read and write.
existingExample: Improving adult literacy can transform the economic prospects of rural communities.

definitionEn: how well a student does in their studies.
existingExample: There is growing evidence that sleep has a direct impact on academic performance.

definitionEn: the ability to analyse information objectively and make a reasoned judgement.
existingExample: Debate clubs help students develop critical thinking and confidence.

definitionEn: done in addition to the normal course of study.
existingExample: Extracurricular activities such as sport and music teach children teamwork.

definitionEn: the practice of training people to obey rules and control their behaviour.
existingExample: Teachers often struggle to maintain discipline in overcrowded classrooms.

definitionEn: education at university or college level.
meaningVi: giáo dục đại học, sau phổ thông
existingExample: Access to tertiary education should depend on ability rather than wealth.

definitionEn: money given to a student to help pay for their education.
existingExample: She won a full scholarship to study engineering abroad.

definitionEn: a way of studying from home, usually online, without attending classes in person.
existingExample: Distance learning gives working adults the flexibility to study at their own pace.

definitionEn: the percentage of students who leave school or a course before finishing.
existingExample: Free school meals have helped to reduce the dropout rate in poorer areas.

definitionEn: including students of different levels of ability.
existingExample: Teaching mixed-ability classes requires careful planning.

definitionEn: the process of judging how well someone has learned something.
existingExample: Continuous assessment may give a fairer picture of a student's ability than a single exam.

definitionEn: the methods and theory of teaching.
existingExample: Many teacher-training programmes now emphasise student-centred pedagogy.

definitionEn: having a wide range of skills, interests and experience.
existingExample: Schools should aim to produce well-rounded individuals, not just high scorers.

definitionEn: influence from people of your own age to behave like them.
existingExample: Teenagers often succumb to peer pressure to fit in with their classmates.

definitionEn: to study very hard for a short time before an exam.
existingExample: Students who cram the night before an exam rarely retain the information.

definitionEn: to officially join a course or school.
existingExample: More adults are enrolling on part-time courses to update their skills.

definitionEn: to gain knowledge or a skill.
existingExample: Young children acquire languages more easily than adults.

definitionEn: a clear understanding of something; to understand something completely.
existingExample: A firm grasp of basic maths is essential for everyday life.

definitionEn: a test given and scored in the same way for all students.
existingExample: Critics argue that standardised tests measure memory rather than intelligence.

definitionEn: a system in which people succeed because of ability rather than wealth or class.
meaningVi: chế độ trọng dụng nhân tài
existingExample: Scholarships help make higher education more of a meritocracy.

definitionEn: learning in which students investigate questions themselves.
meaningVi: học tập dựa trên khám phá
existingExample: Inquiry-based learning encourages pupils to ask their own questions.

definitionEn: a period of on-the-job training with a skilled worker.
meaningVi: chương trình học nghề (vừa học vừa làm)
existingExample: Apprenticeships allow young people to earn while they learn.

definitionEn: the difference in results between groups of students.
meaningVi: khoảng cách thành tích học tập
existingExample: Tutoring programmes aim to close the attainment gap between rich and poor pupils.

definitionEn: a family situation with little money or opportunity.
existingExample: Students from disadvantaged backgrounds are less likely to attend university.

definitionEn: money borrowed to pay for university study.
existingExample: Many graduates spend years repaying their student loans.

definitionEn: the degree to which graduates have the skills employers want.
meaningVi: khả năng có việc làm của sinh viên tốt nghiệp
existingExample: Work placements can improve graduate employability.

definitionEn: involving practical experience rather than theory.
existingExample: Science is best taught through hands-on experiments.

definitionEn: based on ideas rather than real, physical things.
existingExample: Young children find abstract concepts such as time difficult.

definitionEn: students' ability to take control of their own learning.
meaningVi: tính tự chủ của người học
existingExample: Online courses demand a high degree of learner autonomy.

definitionEn: the desire to do something because it is interesting or satisfying in itself.
existingExample: Excessive rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation.

definitionEn: coming from outside, such as rewards or punishments.
existingExample: Prizes are an extrinsic motivator whose effect may not last.

definitionEn: honesty in academic work, without cheating or copying.
existingExample: AI writing tools pose new challenges to academic integrity.

definitionEn: presenting someone else's work as your own.
existingExample: Universities use software to detect plagiarism.

definitionEn: to change a system completely in order to improve it.
existingExample: The government plans to overhaul the national curriculum.

definitionEn: the list of topics covered in a course.
existingExample: Teachers struggle to cover the entire syllabus before exams.

definitionEn: work done during a course that counts towards the final grade.
meaningVi: bài tập tính điểm trong khóa học
existingExample: Coursework rewards steady effort rather than exam technique.

definitionEn: very careful and demanding high standards.
existingExample: Medical students undergo rigorous training.

definitionEn: having exceptional intellectual ability.
existingExample: Special programmes can stretch academically gifted pupils.

definitionEn: dividing students into classes according to ability.
existingExample: Critics argue that streaming labels children too early.

definitionEn: where the teacher talks and students mainly listen.
meaningVi: lấy giáo viên làm trung tâm
existingExample: Teacher-centred lessons can leave students passive.

definitionEn: focused on students' needs and active participation.
meaningVi: lấy người học làm trung tâm
existingExample: Student-centred learning encourages discussion and collaboration.

definitionEn: educating children at home instead of at school.
existingExample: Some parents opt for home-schooling to tailor lessons to their child.

definitionEn: a school for only boys or only girls.
meaningVi: trường chỉ dành cho một giới
existingExample: Some studies suggest that girls perform better in single-sex schools.

definitionEn: teaching boys and girls together.
existingExample: Co-educational schools reflect the mixed nature of society.

definitionEn: extra lessons that families pay for privately.
existingExample: Private tuition is extremely common in many Asian countries.

definitionEn: focused mainly on passing examinations.
existingExample: An exam-oriented system may discourage creativity.

definitionEn: the growth of a child's ability to think and understand.
existingExample: Reading aloud supports young children's cognitive development.

definitionEn: education for children before they start primary school.
existingExample: Investment in early childhood education yields long-term benefits.

definitionEn: the ability to understand and work with numbers.
existingExample: Basic numeracy is essential for managing personal finances.

definitionEn: skills that are useful in many different jobs.
existingExample: Team projects build transferable skills such as communication.

definitionEn: personal skills such as communication and teamwork.
existingExample: Employers complain that many graduates lack soft skills.

definitionEn: combining two or more academic subjects.
existingExample: Climate studies require an interdisciplinary approach.

definitionEn: an experienced person who advises a less experienced one.
existingExample: Mentoring schemes pair new teachers with experienced colleagues.

definitionEn: a natural ability to do something.
existingExample: She showed an early aptitude for languages.

definitionEn: existing from birth.
existingExample: Some people believe intelligence is largely innate.

definitionEn: to help something develop; the care given to a child.
existingExample: Schools should nurture creativity, not merely test it.

definitionEn: to encourage something to develop.
meaningVi: thúc đẩy, khuyến khích phát triển
existingExample: Group projects foster cooperation between students.

definitionEn: to prevent something from developing.
existingExample: Overly strict rules can stifle students' creativity.

definitionEn: to gradually make someone have a quality or feeling.
existingExample: Parents try to instil good habits in their children.

definitionEn: to pass on knowledge or skills.
existingExample: A good teacher imparts knowledge in an engaging way.

definitionEn: eager to learn and ask questions.
existingExample: Inquisitive children ask endless questions about the world.

definitionEn: careful to do work well and thoroughly.
existingExample: Conscientious students rarely miss deadlines.

definitionEn: showing care and steady effort.
existingExample: Diligent revision is more effective than last-minute study.

definitionEn: to perform less well than your ability suggests.
existingExample: Bright pupils may underachieve if they are not challenged.

definitionEn: staying away from school without permission.
existingExample: Truancy is often linked to problems at home.

definitionEn: to officially make someone leave a school.
existingExample: He was expelled for repeated bullying.

definitionEn: repeatedly hurting or frightening a weaker person.
existingExample: Schools must have clear anti-bullying policies.

definitionEn: a young person who has just finished school.
meaningVi: học sinh vừa rời ghế phổ thông
existingExample: Many school leavers now choose apprenticeships over university.

definitionEn: a year off between school and university.
meaningVi: năm nghỉ trước khi vào đại học
existingExample: A gap year can help students mature before university.

definitionEn: relating to study after a first degree.
meaningVi: sau đại học; học viên sau đại học
existingExample: Postgraduate degrees are increasingly required for research posts.

definitionEn: a university student studying for a first degree.
existingExample: Undergraduates often share accommodation in their first year.

definitionEn: a department of a university; its academic staff.
existingExample: Faculty members are expected to publish research.

definitionEn: a long piece of writing for a degree; a main argument.
existingExample: She is writing her thesis on urban migration.

definitionEn: official approval that a course meets required standards.
existingExample: The course has gained international accreditation.

definitionEn: respected and admired.
existingExample: Graduates of prestigious universities often earn higher salaries.

definitionEn: a situation in which academics are cut off from ordinary life.
existingExample: Universities are sometimes criticised as ivory towers.

definitionEn: the highest level of education someone has completed.
meaningVi: trình độ học vấn đạt được
existingExample: Educational attainment strongly predicts lifetime earnings.

definitionEn: the inability to read and write.
existingExample: Adult education programmes aim to eradicate illiteracy.

definitionEn: combining online study with face-to-face teaching.
meaningVi: học kết hợp (trực tuyến + trực tiếp)
existingExample: Blended learning combines the flexibility of online study with classroom support.

definitionEn: a model where students study content at home and practise in class.
existingExample: In a flipped classroom, lectures are watched at home.

definitionEn: a free online course open to anyone (massive open online course).
meaningVi: khóa học trực tuyến đại trà
existingExample: MOOCs give millions of people access to university-level teaching.

definitionEn: qualifications that show you are suitable for something.
existingExample: Employers increasingly look beyond academic credentials.

definitionEn: an economy based on information and skills rather than manufacturing.
existingExample: Education is crucial to competing in the knowledge economy.

definitionEn: to give someone the skills they need.
existingExample: Schools should equip students with practical life skills.

definitionEn: to develop a skill, quality or interest.
existingExample: Libraries help children cultivate a love of reading.

definitionEn: to make something wider or more varied.
existingExample: Studying abroad broadens students' horizons.

definitionEn: having a lot of knowledge about a subject.
existingExample: Education produces well-informed citizens who can judge policies.

definitionEn: to repeat information without understanding it.
existingExample: Examinations that merely reward students who regurgitate memorised facts fail to assess genuine understanding.

definitionEn: the tendency for grades to rise without a real rise in standards.
existingExample: Grade inflation makes it harder for employers to compare candidates.

definitionEn: a list ranking schools or universities by performance.
existingExample: Schools may focus on exam results to climb league tables.

definitionEn: support for students' personal and emotional well-being.
meaningVi: sự chăm sóc tinh thần học sinh
existingExample: Good pastoral care helps students cope with stress.

definitionEn: learning difficulties or disabilities that require extra support.
meaningVi: nhu cầu giáo dục đặc biệt
existingExample: Teachers need training to support pupils with special educational needs.

definitionEn: teaching students of all abilities and backgrounds together.
existingExample: Inclusive education allows disabled children to learn alongside their peers.

definitionEn: practical training for a particular job.
existingExample: Vocational training can reduce youth unemployment.
